paragraphs.text: For in the last days false prophets shall be multiplied, and such as corrupt the word; and the sheep shall be changed into wolves, and love into hatred: for through the abounding of iniquity the love of many shall wax cold. For men shall hate, and persecute, and betray one another. And then shall appear the deceiver of the world, the enemy of the truth, the prince of lies, [2 Thessalonians 2:3-12] whom the Lord Jesus "shall destroy with the spirit of His mouth, who takes away the wicked with His lips; and many shall be offended at Him. But they that endure to the end, the same shall be saved.
paragraphs.author: Apostolic Constitutions

paragraphs.text: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven;" [Isaiah 11:4; Matthew 24:1-51] and afterwards shall be the voice of a trumpet by the archangel; and in that interval shall be the revival of those that were asleep. And then shall the Lord come, and all His saints with Him, with a great concussion above the clouds, with the angels of His power, [Matthew 16:27] in the throne of His kingdom, to condemn the devil, the deceiver of the world, and to render to every one according to his deeds.
paragraphs.author: Apostolic Constitutions

paragraphs.text: "Then shall the wicked go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous shall go into life eternal," [Matthew 25:46] to inherit those things "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, such things as God has prepared for them that love Him;" [1 Corinthians 2:9] and they shall rejoice in the kingdom of God, which is in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs.author: Apostolic Constitutions

paragraphs.text: Then when he had passed sentence on the temple, his disciples who were still under the influence of Judaic sentiment were sorrow-struck; and scripture afterwards says: When descending from the Mount they showed him the building of the temple, in order no doubt that they might move him to pity, and that he might recall what he had said with regard to the temple, for they knew and believed that everything spoken by him would come to pass. But he knowing [what would be] said to them: Do you see all these things?
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: Verily, I say unto you, there shall not be left here one stone, upon another that shall not be thrown down. Then were they possessed with fear, and remained silent, and said nothing further on this matter. Accordingly thereafter came the Romans, and levelled with the ground the temple and the city, and made it an utter desolation, executing as if by compact what had been commanded by the Lord. And up to this day we see with our very eyes that lo! for more than five hundred years it has lain so desolate that it cannot be renovated.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: Some were pointing out to Christ the magnificent things in the temple and how it was adorned by the gifts that had been dedicated to God. For they supposed that Jesus would admire with them all there was to see, although being God he has heaven as his throne! He does offer a teaching concerning them, but he had already predicted that according to the times the temple would utterly fall. The Roman army is being gathered for this very thing, demanding the surrender of Israel itself as all Jerusalem suffers the punishment of the slaying of the Lord. For let me tell you, it came to pass that they suffered these things after the crucifixion of the Savior. But they did not understand the meaning of Jesus' teachings. They supposed his teachings concerned the consummation of the age.
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Figuratively; When the Lord departed from the temple, all the buildings of the Law and the structure of the Commandments were so overthrown, that none of them could be fulfilled by the Jews, but, the Head being taken away, all the parts were at war among themselves.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Chapter 24 - Verses 1, 2.) And Jesus went out of the temple and was going on his way. And his disciples came to show him the buildings of the temple. But he answered and said to them: Do you see all these things? Amen I say to you: there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone, that shall not be destroyed. According to the manifest sense of the story, when the Lord departed from the temple, all the buildings of the law, and the composition of the commandments, were so destroyed that nothing could be fulfilled by the Jews; and with the head removed, all the members fight among themselves.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: For inasmuch as He said, "Your house is left desolate," and had previously forewarned them of many grievous things; therefore the disciples having heard these things, as though marvelling at it, came unto Him, showing the beauty of the temple, and wondering, if so much beauty was to be destroyed, and materials so costly, and variety of workmanship past utterance; He no longer thenceforth talks to them of desolation merely, but foretells an entire destruction. "See ye not all these things," saith He, and do ye marvel, and are ye amazed? "There shall not remain one stone upon another." How then did it remain? one may say. But what is this? For neither so hath the prediction fallen to the ground. For He said these things either indicating its entire desolation, or at that spot where He was. For there are parts of it destroyed unto the foundations.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: And together with its we would say another thing also, that from what hath been done, even the most contentious ought to believe concerning the remains, that they are utterly to be destroyed.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: And Jesus went out from the temple and was departing; and his disciples came to him, to show him the buildings of the temple. But Jesus answering said to them: do you see all these things? amen I say to you, there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone that shall not be destroyed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After Christ had foretold all the things that were to come upon Jerusalem, he went out from the temple — he who had preserved the temple, lest it fall, so long as he was in it. For as long as the Word was among the Jews, not taking the kingdom of God away from them, so long it stood, and the affairs of the Jews were unharmed. But after, according to his own word which he had spoken: "the kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and shall be given to a nation producing its own fruit", he took away the kingdom of God and gave it to the Gentiles, then both Jesus and the kingdom of God came to be among the Gentiles. Hence now neither Jesus nor the kingdom of God is held among the Jews, because they have been left "like a tabernacle in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber-field, and like a city that is besieged", on account of the crime which they committed against Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And each one who receives the word of God is a temple of God, so that it may rightly be said to him: "Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" Each one therefore, since he is a holy temple of God because of the Spirit of God dwelling within him, if he himself sins, becomes the cause of his own desertion, so that Christ goes out from him, so that he who had before been a temple of the Son of God is thereafter a deserted house, so that there is not left in him a stone upon a stone — out of all the doctrines and edifications of a good life — that is not destroyed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: On account of which, calling to mind the history of the desertion of Jerusalem, we ought to look out for ourselves, that Christ not go out from the temple (which is made up of us), that the buildings of our temple may be unharmed, adorned with stones and gifts, so that those who see the buildings that are in us may say in wonder: "see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But this is worthy to be examined thoroughly, how, as far as the text goes, the disciples speak thus to Jesus, and show him the buildings of stones, as though someone who had never seen the temple itself but had come from elsewhere as a stranger arriving for the first time. To this it must be answered thus: that when above, prophesying its coming ruin, Christ had thus threatened its desertion: "behold, now your house shall be left to you deserted", the disciples, hearing it, marveled that such and so great a building of the temple was to be reduced to nothing. Therefore they say to Jesus (as another evangelist says more plainly): "master, do you see what kind of stones and what kind of buildings", namely so that they might bend him to mercy for that place, that he not do what he had threatened to do.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And let these things be understood in a bodily sense; but morally in this way: since the marvelous construction of human nature has been made — namely, the temple of God and of his Word — the disciples and the other saints (not only then, but even now confessing the wondrous works of God toward the human creature) intercede before the sight of Christ and appeal to Christ, that he may not abandon the human race on account of their sins, but rather that his wondrous works may move him to indulgence more than their iniquities move him to wrath.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Otherwise: just as that temple was not demolished all at once but little by little as time went on, so also every man who takes into himself the Word of God is a temple; and if indeed after sin he has not fallen away wholly from the Word of God, but still preserves in part the traces of faith and of the religious keeping of God's commandments within himself, he is a temple in part destroyed and in part still standing. But whoever, after he has sinned, takes no care of himself, but is ever running away from faith and from the life which is according to the Gospel, is diminished little by little, until he wholly withdraws "from the living God" — this man is a temple in which there shall not be left a stone of doctrine upon a stone of God's commandments that shall not be thrown down. We, therefore, ought to look out for ourselves, that the whole building of piety may remain intact within us, so that, both adorned with the stones of saving doctrines and decorated with the gifts of good works, we may take into ourselves the power and glory of God, and Christ, who is the Word and Wisdom of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And someone introduces a third exposition of this kind: that the temple of God was built by a composition of words that carry meaning, namely the whole Scripture of the Old Testament constructed according to its history. Those who constructed it — Moses or the prophets — by the setting-together of letters and the ordering of sayings, built it to be admired by all for the beauty of its stones, that is, of the choice sayings and of the sense-meanings to be praised as gifts.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This the disciples point out to Jesus, taking up all the Scriptures; and to them Christ replies, saying that this bodily and first building is to be destroyed by the Word, so that a more divine and more mysterious temple of another Scripture may be built.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: That the Scripture is a temple was expounded by someone before us. And since the Antichrist — "he who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God", who sits in the temple of God — is the false word that is held in the Scriptures — which counterfeits the truth by bringing forward, out of the Scriptures, testimonies of impious teachings, when men are unwilling to be won over from any other source; and this very thing is "that which opposes", and it sits both upon the seat of the Scriptures and upon their building, "displaying itself as though it were God". And one may always see the words of the heresies, as Antichrists, sitting in the temple of the Scriptures and wishing, out of those very Scriptures, to win over those who hear them, as though each one of these were itself God the Word in the Scriptures.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Christ, when He had foretold all that should come upon Jerusalem, went forth out of the temple, He, who while He was in it, had upheld the temple that it should not fall. And so each man, being the temple of God by reason of the Spirit of God dwelling in him, is himself the cause of his being deserted, that Christ should depart from him. It is worthy of note how they show Him the buildings of the temple, as though He had never seen them. We reply, that when Christ had foretold the destruction that should come upon the temple, His disciples were amazed at the thought that so magnificent buildings should be utterly ruined, and therefore they show them to Him to move Him to pity, that He would not do what He had threatened. And because the constitution of human nature is wonderful, being made the temple of God, the disciples and the rest of the saints confessing the wonderful working of God in respect of the forming of men, intercede before the face of Christ, that He would not forsake the human race for their sins.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The historical sense is clear, that in the forty-second year after the Lord's passion, the city and temple were overthrown under the Roman Emperors Vespasian and Titus.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: So it was ordained of God, that as soon as the light of grace was revealed, the temple with its ceremonies should be taken out of the way, lest any weakling in the faith, beholding all the things instituted of the Lord and hallowed by the Prophets yet abiding, might be gradually drawn away from the purity of the faith to a carnal Judaism.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: The magnificent splendor of the temple's design was shown to Christ immediately after he had warned of Jerusalem's desolation, as though to move him. Yet he said that everything had to be destroyed and the scattered stones of its entire foundation demolished, for an eternal temple was being consecrated as a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. This eternal temple is the man who is made worthy of becoming God's habitation through knowledge of the Son, confession of the Father and obedience to the commandments.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: Every man also, who, by taking into him the word of God, is become a temple, if after sinning he yet retains in part the traces of faith and religion, his temple is in part destroyed, and in part standing. But he who after sin has no regard for himself is gradually alienated, until he has altogether forsaken the living God, and so one stone is not left upon another of God's commandments, which he has not thrown down.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Watch for your life's sake. Let not your lamps be quenched, nor your loins unloosed; but be ye ready, for ye know not the hour in which our Lord cometh.
paragraphs.author: Didache

paragraphs.text: But often shall ye come together, seeking the things which are befitting to your souls: for the whole time of your faith will not profit you, if ye be not made perfect in the last time. For in the last days false prophets and corrupters shall be multiplied, and the sheep shall be turned into wolves, and love shall be turned into hate; for when lawlessness increaseth, they shall hate and persecute and betray one another, and then shall appear the world-deceiver as Son of God, and shall do signs and wonders, and the earth shall be delivered into his hands, and he shall do iniquitous things which have never yet come to pass since the beginning.
paragraphs.author: Didache

paragraphs.text: Then shall the creation of men come into the fire of trial, and many shall be made to stumble and shall perish; but they that endure in their faith shall be saved from under the curse itself. And then shall appear the signs of the truth; first, the sign of an out-spreading in heaven; then the sign of the sound of the trumpet; and the third, the resurrection of the dead; yet not of all, but as it is said: The Lord shall come and all His saints with Him. Then shall the world see the Lord coming upon the clouds of heaven.
paragraphs.author: Didache

paragraphs.text: And because the questions of the disciples are threefold, they are separated by different times and meanings. That concerning the destruction of the city is first answered, and is then confirmed by truth of doctrine, that no seducer might prevail with the ignorant.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Vers. 3, 4.) But while he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying: Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age? And Jesus answered them, saying: See that no one deceives you. He sits on the Mount of Olives, where the true light of knowledge was born, and the disciples come to him privately, who desired to know the mysteries and revelations of the future, and they ask three things: When will Jerusalem be destroyed; when will Christ come; when will the end of the age be.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: They ask Him three things. First, The time of the destruction of Jerusalem, saying, Tell us when shall these things be? Secondly, The time of Christ's coming, saying, And what shall be the sign of Thy coming? Thirdly, The time of the consummation of this world, saying, And of the end of the world?
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "And as He sat upon the mount of Olives, the disciples came unto Him privately, saying, Tell us when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of Thy coming, and of the end of the world?"
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Therefore did they come unto Him privately, as it was of such matters they meant to inquire. For they were in travail to know the day of His coming, because of their eager desire to behold that glory, which is the cause of countless blessings. And these two things do they ask him, when shall these things be? that is, the overthrow of the temple; and, what is the sign of thy coming? But Luke saith, the question was one concerning Jerusalem, as though they were supposing that then is His coming. And Mark saith, that neither did all of them ask concerning the end of Jerusalem, but Peter and John, as having greater freedom of speech.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: I think Mount Olivet to be a mystery of the Church out of the Gentiles.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the husbandman dwelling on Mount Olivet is the word of God confirmed in the Church, that is, Christ, who ever grafts the branches of the wild olive on the good olive tree of the Fathers. They who have confidence before Christ, seek to learn the sign of the coming of Christ, and of the consummation of this world. And the coming of the Word into the soul is of two sorts. The first is that foolish preaching concerning Christ, when we preach that Christ was born and crucified; the second its coming in perfect men, concerning which it is said, We speak wisdom among them that are perfect; (1 Cor. 2:6.) and to this second coming is added the end of the world in the perfect man to whom the world is crucified.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But as he was sitting upon the Mount of Olives, his disciples came to him privately, saying: tell us, when shall these things be, and what shall be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "When Jesus had gone out of the temple", after he had spoken concerning it, he came to the Mount of Olives and there sat with his disciples. But I think that the Mount of Olives is a mystery of the Church which is from the Gentiles, in which olive trees have been planted, each one of which can say: "but I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God". And perhaps too on this Mount of Olives the roots of the good olive tree are present, but the branches of the wild olive have been grafted in in the place of the branches which "were cut off through unbelief". And the husbandman residing on the Mount of Olives is the Word of God confirmed in the Church, Christ, who is ever grafting the branches of the wild olive into the good olive tree of the fathers, of Moses and of the rest of the prophets, so that, receiving richness from the holy prophets (through this, that they carefully understand their meaning, and receive also the Christ who is prophesied by them), they may offer abundant and richer fruit—than, that is to say, the former olives, which because of the curse that was in the law have been shaken down, so that they can no longer be of use.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: After this it must be considered that, of the disciples approaching Jesus, some indeed approach him privately, having in this very thing greater confidence with him as those of his household (as when they questioned him about the solving of the parables), but others questioned him not privately but in common. Observe further the difference between these, that at times indeed the Pharisees approach, whether tempting him or questioning him in whatever manner, but at other times others desiring to learn—yet these never approach privately out of the multitude.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And perhaps even now those who have taken up a distinguished life and on account of this have confidence before Christ, having something more than those who from the common faith approach Jesus, say to him: tell us, when shall these things be? these things—which? that which he said: "there shall not stand here one stone upon a stone which shall not be destroyed". And they wish to learn not only this, but also the sign of the coming of Christ and of the consummation of the age; and two things they ask of him, the sign of his coming and of the consummation of the age. Therefore the coming of the Son of God and the consummation of the age is indeed believed among many, but especially among those who pursue a more refined life.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It is possible also in another way to see a twofold coming of Christ, that is, the coming of the Word into the soul. First indeed the untrained and those then beginning to know Christ, because they cannot see the brightness of his beauty, say: "we saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness, but his appearance was without honor". Now the unhonored appearance of the Word is the foolish preaching about Christ, when we preach Christ born and crucified. But the second coming is the coming of Christ among perfect men, concerning whom the steward of his word says: "but we speak wisdom among the perfect".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And these perfect ones have become lovers of his beauty and beseech the Word, that he gird upon himself his rational sword and set it about the mystery of the fleshly nativity, which is called mystically the thigh. For disciples of this kind praise the beauty and comeliness of the Word, and to this second coming is joined the consummation of the age in the man coming to perfection and saying: "but far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world". For if the world has been crucified to the just, to whom "the world has been crucified", then the consummation of the world has also been made for them. Necessarily, therefore, those who have the confidence of approaching privately to Christ wish to learn the sign of the coming of Christ and of the consummation of the age, so that, being benefited by this—that they have learned the coming of Christ and the consummation—they may show themselves worthy to see his second coming and the consummation of the age according to what we have handed down.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The Lord continuing His walk arrives at Mount Olivet, having by the way foretold the destruction of the temple to those disciples who had shown and commended the buildings. When they had reached the Mount they came to Him, asking Him further of this.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: For Mount Olivet has no unfruitful trees, but olives, which supply light to dispel darkness, which give rest to the weary, health to the sick. And sitting on Mount Olivet over against the temple, the Lord discourses of its destruction, and the destruction of the Jewish nation, that even by His choice of a situation He might show, that abiding still in the Church He condemns the pride of the wicked.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: And so, if the manifestation of the Lord's kingdom pertains unto the will of God and unto our anxious expectation, how do some pray for some protraction of the age, when the kingdom of God, which we pray may arrive, tends unto the consummation of the age? Our wish is, that our reign be hastened, not our servitude protracted.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: What then saith He? "Take heed that no man deceive you. For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ, and shall deceive many. And ye shall hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that ye be not troubled; for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: For since they felt as being told of vengeance falling on others when hearing of that which was to be brought upon Jerusalem and as though they were to be out of the turmoils, and were dreaming of good things only, and looked for these to befall them quite immediately; for this cause He again foretells to them grievous things, making them earnest, and commanding them on two grounds to watch, so as neither to be seduced by the deceit of them that would beguile them, nor to be overpowered by the violence of ills that should overtake them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But He answered nothing directly to this question, but first speaks of those other things that are urgent, and which it was needful for them to learn first. For neither concerning Jerusalem straightway, nor of His own second coming, did He speak, but touching the ills that were to meet them at the doors. Wherefore also He makes them earnest in their exertions, by saying, "Take heed that no man deceive you; for many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Afterwards, when He hath roused them to listen about these things (for, "take heed," saith He, "that no man deceive you"); and having made them energetic, and prepared them to be watchful, and hath spoken first of the false Christs, then He speaks of the ills of Jerusalem, assuring them ever by the things already past, foolish and contentious though they were, of those which were yet to come.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: And Jesus answering said to them: See that no one seduces you. For many will come in my name saying that I am the Christ, and they will seduce many (24, 4. 5).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Those who understand simply suppose that these words signify only this: that many were going to come asserting themselves to be Christs, having in themselves also certain wonder-working powers and words by which they might provoke to belief many who had shown themselves worthy of seduction. But John in his epistle says: "and as you have heard that Antichrist is coming, now many Antichrists have arisen; whence we know that it is the last hour". By these words he teaches that every word which is foreign to the truth and asserts itself to be the word of God is Antichrist; for it is thus possible to understand what he says: "and now many Antichrists have arisen", since there is one thing that is true. But as the record of the readings makes plain, there were not many men in the time of the apostles who said that they were Christs, unless perhaps Dositheus the Samaritan — whence they are also called Dositheans — and Simon, of whom the Acts report, who proclaimed himself to be the great power of God. Besides these, there were none either before or afterward, so far as my knowledge goes.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But every discourse which professes an exposition of the Scriptures and faith in them, yet does not have the truth, is rightly to be understood to be Antichrist, coming in the name of Christ and saying that I am the Christ, lying and by no means able to display in itself the form of truth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And since to those who examine the words of Scripture, in order to find its meaning, there frequently occur certain interpretations as if true when they are not true, and sometimes they are drawn also by other plausible, specious discourses, so that it is not easy to find which is the true meaning before against the lying estimations the truer and firmer meaning has been found — for this reason I think that Christ, to the question of his disciples saying: "when shall these things be? and what is the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?" answered thus: See that no one seduces you. For many will come in my name saying: I am the Christ, and they will seduce many. For truly he who fulfills that commandment which says: "be prudent money-changers", and that which says: "prove all things, hold fast what is good; abstain yourselves from every evil appearance", will see many being seduced by false interpretations and words professing themselves to be Christ the word of God. And would that only those who are outside the Church were seduced: it would be easy to guard against the seduction.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But now those very people who profess themselves to be churchmen are deceived and seduced about various necessary chapters, as their very dissension is a testimony, since even those who are within are seduced.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But consequently, just as it is wont to be among those wandering these bodily roads that there is a difference of error, and some indeed even go against the very public road that is sought, wandering, while others turn aside a little something from the straight path so that they may be recalled, and there are many differences among those who wander — in this manner we see also those who stray from the truth. And the Marcionites indeed and Basilides, and the Valentinians and the Apellians and the Ophites wander much from the proposed way, since they hold opinions wholly contrary to the truth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But some do not indeed dissent about the public and manifest chapters — for instance, about the one God who gave the Law and the Gospel, or about Christ Jesus the firstborn of every creature, who at the end of the age according to the preachings of the prophets came into the world and took upon himself the true nature of human flesh, so that he even underwent birth from a virgin, and took upon himself the death of the cross and rose from the dead and deified the human nature which he had taken up. Furthermore also about the Holy Spirit, that he himself was the one in the patriarchs and prophets who afterward was given in the apostles, and about the resurrection of the dead as the Gospel teaches they most certainly believe, and all things whatsoever are handed down in the churches.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But about other things not few, yet slight, they propose new dogmas, and they too indeed are among those who are seduced by false interpretations and words coming in the name of Christ, who is the word and the truth. And it is an evil indeed to find someone erring according to the conduct of life, but I think it is much worse to go astray in dogmas and not to hold opinions according to the truest rule of the Scriptures. For if for moral sins we are to be punished, still more those sinning through false dogmas.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For if a good conduct of morals sufficed for men unto salvation, how is it that among the Gentiles many philosophers, or among the heretics many living continently, are by no means saved, as though the falsity of their dogma obscured and defiled their conduct?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I think that the discourse, wishing to show a general cleanness which is not only in acts but also in knowledge, says in the twenty-third Psalm: who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? he that is innocent in hands and pure in heart, and in the Proverbs: who shall boast that he has a chaste heart? or who shall be confident that he is clean from sins? I therefore think that the one clean in heart and chaste in heart is no other than he who possesses a heart clean and chaste from every false dogma; so also I reckon him to be innocent in hands and clean from sins who is irreproachable in the acts of his life. And it must be known that (as regards the truth) it is impossible for anyone to be innocent in hands and clean from sins without being pure in heart and chaste from false dogmas; just as, on the contrary, it is impossible to be clean indeed and chaste in heart from false dogmas without being innocent in "hands" and clean from sins. For these follow one another mutually and are not separated from each other: a discourse clean in the soul and a life irreproachable.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But we have treated this chapter more abundantly, teaching ourselves according to what has seemed good to us in the passage, that we may keep ourselves from every error of false dogmas, whether about the manifest and principal chapters or about those which seem lesser, that we may hear him who said: "you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left", from him who said: "I am the way", and that we may not be seduced, but may keep watch lest any of those deceive us who come in the name of Christ saying: I am the Christ, I am the truth and wisdom and the true light.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I think that not only is discourse Christ and feigned discourse Antichrist, truth Christ and feigned truth Antichrist, wisdom Christ and feigned wisdom Antichrist (deceiving the lovers of the wisdom of God and of truth, all of which pertain to the account of faith), but also in these virtues by which we live according to God, we find that all the virtues are Christ and all the feigned virtues Antichrist, since all the kinds of good, whatsoever Christ has in himself in truth for the edification of men, all of these the devil has in himself in appearance for the seduction of the saints.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For thus Christ is righteousness, yet "there are" frequently "ways of a man which seem to be righteous, but the last of them look down into the depth of hell". When therefore something seems to be righteousness, while it is not true righteousness, such righteousness is Antichrist against Christ who is righteousness. I think also that there is a chastity that is Antichrist, which is among the heretics sending men into error, that they may not understand the ecclesiastical chastity which is Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: So also there is a mercy that is Antichrist against the mercy which is Christ, in those who give alms, but not for the sake of the righteousness of God. There is also a patience that is Antichrist in those who indeed seem to suffer for Christianity and "striving even to the shedding of blood", that is, lest they seem to deny Christianity; yet in that very shedding of their blood they "speak iniquity on high", and set "their mouth in heaven".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: There is also a power that is Antichrist seducing the ignorant, since many are going to say to Christ in that day: "Lord, in your name we cast out demons, and did many powerful works", to whom he will answer: "depart from me, all you who work iniquity, I never knew you". For if Christ never knew them, yet they boast that they did powerful works in the name of Christ, those powers were not from Christ who had not known them, but from him who "transfigures himself" not only "into an angel of light" but even into Christ himself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: There is need therefore for us of God as helper and of Christ himself living in us, that with our eyes opened we may see, lest anyone seduce us — either a discourse or a power, whether from within or from without — promising itself to be Christ, when it is his enemy and the enemy of his other virtues.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Consider also this, that many come in nothing else but in my name; for Antichrist takes up only the name of Christ, and neither does the works nor teaches the words of his truth nor displays his wisdom in himself. And just as (according to some) Barabbas too was called Jesus, but was a robber having nothing of Jesus except the name, so I reckon there are many Christs, but in name only. Note, however, that nowhere in the Scriptures is the Lord found using this very expression and saying: I am the Christ, so that he might say nothing similar to the many who were going to come in his name and to say: I am the Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For there sufficed for him, unto the faith of believers (that he himself is the Christ), the works of God, which Christ alone could do, and the discourse which he taught and the power, above a thousand voices crying out: I am the Christ. And thus he never openly said: I am, but he said it through works and through the teaching of piety, so that he himself says to Peter, as to one who had never heard it from him but had learned from the Father, that he himself was "the Christ, the Son of the living God": "blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because not flesh and blood revealed it to you, but my Father who is in the heavens". For if he himself, while set in the body, had openly said to him: I am the Christ, flesh would have seemed to have revealed it to him, and not the Father only. Therefore it suffices for the seduction of the Antichrists this alone which they say: I am the Christ, which Christ is never read to have said, and there are many who are seduced; "for wide is the gate and spacious the way that leads to perdition, and many enter through it"; but few are those who find that way "which leads to life".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The character of the times in which we live is such as to call forth from us even this admonition, that we ought not to be astonished at the heresies (which abound) neither ought their existence to surprise us, for it was foretold that they should come to pass; nor the fact that they subvert the faith of some, for their final cause is, by affording a trial to faith, to give it also the opportunity of being "approved.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: (Verse 5.) For many will come in my name, saying: I am the Christ, and they will deceive many. One of them is Simon the Samaritan, whom we read about in the Acts of the Apostles, who claimed to be a great power of God (Acts 8). Leaving these things aside, he also wrote among other things in his own volumes: I am the word of God, I am beautiful, I am the Paraclete, I am omnipotent, I am all things of God. But even the apostle John speaks in his epistle: You have heard that the Antichrist is coming, now many antichrists are already here (1 John 2:18). I believe that all heresiarchs are Antichrists, and they teach under the name of Christ those things which are contrary to Christ. It is not surprising if we see some being led astray by them, since the Lord has said: And many will be led astray.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: One of them of whom The speaks was Simon of Samaria, of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles, that he gave himself out to be the great Power, leaving these things written in his worksa among others, I am the Word of God, I am the Almighty, I am all things of God. The Apostle John also in his Epistle, Ye have heard that Antichrist shall come; even now there are many Antichrists. (1 John 2:18.) I suppose all heresiarchs to be Antichrists, and under the name of Christ to teach those things which are contrary to Christ. No wonder if we see some led away by such teachers, when the Lord has said, And shall deceive many.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ, and shall deceive many."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: For the war, saith He, shall be twofold that of the deceivers, and that of the enemies, but the former far more grievous, as coming upon them in the confusion and turmoils, and when men were terrified and troubled. For indeed great was the storm then, when the Roman power was beginning to flourish, and cities were taken, and camps and weapons were set in motion, and many were readily believed.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: They that are deceived are many, because wide is the gate that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat. (Mat. 7:13.) This one thing is enough to detect the Antichrists and seducers that they shall say, I am Christ, which Christ Himself is no where read to have said: for the works of God, and the word which He taught, and His power, were enough to produce belief that He is Christ. For every discourse which professes to expound Scripture faithfully, and has not the truth, is Antichrist. For the truth is Christ, that which feigns itself to be the truth is Antichrist.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: So also all virtues are Christ, all that feigns itself to be virtue is Antichrist; for Christ has in Himself in truth all manner of good for the edification of men, but the devil has forged resemblances of the same for the deceiving of the saints. We have need therefore of God to help us, that none deceive us, neither word nor power. It is a bad thing to find any one erring in his course of life; but I esteem it much worse not to think according to the most true rule of Scripture.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (Ep. 199. 25.) To this enquiry of the disciples the Lord makes answer, declaring all things which were to come to pass from that time forwards, whether relating to the destruction of Jerusalem, which had given occasion to their enquiry; or to His coming through the Church, in which He ceases not to come to the end of time; for He is acknowledged as coming among His own, while new members are daily born to Him; or relating to the end itself when He shall appear to judge the quick and the dead. When then He describes the signs which shall attend these three events, we must carefully consider which signs belong to which events, lest perchance we refer to one that which belongs to another.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: Our Lord and Redeemer announces beforehand the evils that precede the perishing world, so that the things to come may disturb us less because they have been foreknown. For missiles that are foreseen strike less forcefully; and we endure the evils of the world more tolerably if we are fortified against them by the shield of foreknowledge. For behold he says: "When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified; for these things must happen first, but the end is not yet at once." The words of our Redeemer must be weighed carefully, through which he announces that we will suffer one thing internally, another externally. For wars indeed pertain to enemies, seditions to citizens. Therefore, to indicate that we are troubled both internally and externally, he declares that we suffer one thing from enemies, another from brothers.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: (Verse 6.) For you will hear of battles and rumors of battles: see that you are not troubled. For these things must happen; but the end is not yet. Therefore, when we see these things happening, let us not think that the day of judgment is imminent, but that it is reserved for that time, whose sign is clearly set forth in the following events.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: That is, Think not that the day of judgment is at hand, but that it is reserved against another time; the sign of which is plainly put in what follows, For nation shall rise against-nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: For the war, saith He, shall be twofold that of the deceivers, and that of the enemies, but the former far more grievous, as coming upon them in the confusion and turmoils, and when men were terrified and troubled. For indeed great was the storm then, when the Roman power was beginning to flourish, and cities were taken, and camps and weapons were set in motion, and many were readily believed.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But of wars in Jerusalem is He speaking; for it is not surely of those without, and everywhere in the world; for what did they care for these? And besides, He would thus say nothing new, if He were speaking of the calamities of the world at large, which are happening always. For before this, were wars, and tumults, and fightings; but He speaks of the Jewish wars coming upon them at no great distance, for henceforth the Roman arms were a matter of anxiety. Since then these things also were sufficient to confound them, He foretells them all.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Then to show that He Himself also will assail the Jews with them, and war on them, He speaks not of battles only, but also of plagues sent from God, famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, showing that the wars also He Himself permitted to come upon them, and that these things do not happen for no purpose according to what has been before the accustomed course of things amongst men, but proceed from the wrath on high.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Therefore He saith, they shall come not by themselves or at once, but with signs. For that the Jews may not say, that they who then believed were the authors of these evils, therefore hath He told them also of the cause of their coming upon them. "For verily I say unto you," He said before, "all these things shall come upon this generation," having made mention of the stain of blood on them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Then lest on hearing of the showers of evils, they should suppose the gospel to be broken through, He added, "See, be not troubled, for all things must come to pass," i.e which I foretold, and the approach of the temptations will set aside none of the things which I have said; but there shall indeed be tumults and confusion, but nothing shall shake my predictions.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Then since He had said to the Jews, "Ye shall not see me, till ye shall say, Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord;" and the disciples supposed that together with the destruction would be the end also; to set right this secret thought of theirs, He said, "But the end is not yet." For that they did suspect even as I said, you may learn from their question. For, what did they ask? When shall these things be? i.e. when shall Jerusalem be destroyed? And what is the sign of Thy coming, and of the end of the world?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But He answered nothing directly to this question, but first speaks of those other things that are urgent, and which it was needful for them to learn first. For neither concerning Jerusalem straightway, nor of His own second coming, did He speak, but touching the ills that were to meet them at the doors. Wherefore also He makes them earnest in their exertions, by saying, "Take heed that no man deceive you; for many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Afterwards, when He hath roused them to listen about these things (for, "take heed," saith He, "that no man deceive you"); and having made them energetic, and prepared them to be watchful, and hath spoken first of the false Christs, then He speaks of the ills of Jerusalem, assuring them ever by the things already past, foolish and contentious though they were, of those which were yet to come.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But by "wars and rumors of wars," He meaneth, what I before said, the troubles coming upon them. After this, because, as I have already said, they supposed after that war the end would come, see how He warns them, saying, "But the end is not yet. For nation," He saith, "shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom." Of the preludes to the ills of the Jews doth He speak. "All these are the beginning of sorrows," that is, of those that befall them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: "And ye shall hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that ye be not troubled; for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But of wars in Jerusalem is He speaking; for it is not surely of those without, and everywhere in the world; for what did they care for these? And besides, He would thus say nothing new, if He were speaking of the calamities of the world at large, which are happening always. For before this, were wars, and tumults, and fightings; but He speaks of the Jewish wars coming upon them at no great distance, for henceforth the Roman arms were a matter of anxiety. Since then these things also were sufficient to confound them, He foretells them all.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Then lest on hearing of the showers of evils, they should suppose the gospel to be broken through, He added, "See, be not troubled, for all things must come to pass," i.e which I foretold, and the approach of the temptations will set aside none of the things which I have said; but there shall indeed be tumults and confusion, but nothing shall shake my predictions.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Then since He had said to the Jews, "Ye shall not see me, till ye shall say, Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord;" and the disciples supposed that together with the destruction would be the end also; to set right this secret thought of theirs, He said, "But the end is not yet." For that they did suspect even as I said, you may learn from their question. For, what did they ask? When shall these things be? i.e. when shall Jerusalem be destroyed? And what is the sign of Thy coming, and of the end of the world?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: To hear the shouts raised in the battles, is to hear wars; to hear rumours of wars, is to hear accounts of wars waged afar off.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This must come to pass before we can see the perfection of that wisdom which is in Christ; but not yet shall be that end which we seek, for a peaceful end is far from those men.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But you shall hear battles and rumors of battles; see that you are not terrified, for these things must happen, but the end is not yet.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Luke, however, puts it this way: "when you hear of battles and seditions, do not be terrified; for these things must first happen, but the end is not at once". In these words he sets forth two things, one thus: you shall hear battles, the other: rumors of battles. And first let us see, according to the simple tradition, in the way that many understand it, how rumors of battles differ from battles. Suppose for me that battles exist where cities rise up against cities or nations against nations, so that the one may carry off the other's property or the stronger may kill the strong. What, then, do rumors of battles signify after battles?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Especially since it is not said: you shall see battles and hear about battles, but on both sides he set you shall hear; that is, both you shall hear battles and you shall hear rumors of battles. And let us suppose that to hear battles is when the sons of peace keep their eyes clean from battles, so that they may not see wicked things; and (since they cannot look upon labors and pains) they hear about battles, what sort of city fights against what sort of city or what sort of nation is stormed by what sort of nation. But what else, besides this, will it be to hear battles and to hear rumors of battles?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: See, then, whether you can (I speak with regard to the simplicity of the word) give such a distinction: it is not one and the same thing to hear from far off, placed away from a battle, that a battle is happening, and to be beside the battle and to hear the very voices of those fighting. Each, therefore, has its own signification. And perhaps he indeed who hears the very voices which are made in battles, hears battles; but he who hears about battles waged far off, hears rumors of battles. For he does not hear the battles themselves.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But since the words are ambiguous, someone may say the reverse, that he who is indeed far from the battles hears about them; while he who is beside the battles hears the rumors of the battles themselves. In both ways, therefore, there seems to be some understanding of the difference.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Rise now to the moral and spiritual understanding, if in any way you can find some interpretation worthy of the eminence of Christ's knowledge and of the subtlety of the evangelists, so that you may not lay aside the dignity of evangelical wisdom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: See therefore whether, recalling those things which were set forth above concerning what he says: many will come in my name saying: I am Christ, and they will lead many astray, we can, according to their sequence, interpret these things also. Everyone therefore who is perfect and sees in his own soul the glorious coming of the Word — which corrupts and consummates the world and crucifies it to the just man, that all worldly things may die to him — and who has senses trained for grasping, must, as he seeks and examines, run into many battles of doctrines.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He will hear also many professing the truth and diverse traditions concerning it, so that, like a good soldier of the Word, he may remain invulnerable in soul against all those professing the truth but not seeing it nor manifesting it, but rather pronouncing things contrary to the truth as though they were the truth; and he may be made worthy to receive into his soul the glorious coming of Christ, according to that whereby he is God the Word, which was in the beginning with God, which is wont to come to those who, after they have known Christ according to the flesh and have received the Word which was made flesh, ascend so far beyond the many that they can grasp not just any sort of glory, but glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And perhaps the Word of God appears in diverse glories, according to the power of each soul that sees, according to the capacity that each single soul has offered. To the one, therefore, who is perfect and has arrived at the consummation of the age, insofar as it depends on him, the Word appears such that whoever has seen him may say: "we have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth". Therefore, if anyone is to be held worthy to receive such a Word and to see it, he must, before a vision of the word of this kind, hear in his soul battles; but through others, who assert as though it were truth whatever has seemed so to them, rumors of battles. And rightly, as his disciples were advancing toward perfection, after the Savior had spoken these things about battles, he added further: see, and did not say: hear, urging them to be watchful, so that they might be able to see with the eyes of the soul (after they have heard battles and rumors of battles) the nature of each of the things that are heard, and, seeing it, not be terrified: because such intelligible battles are wont to arise for righteous men amid diverse persuasions, and to disturb and shake their souls into doubting, lest perhaps those things be true which seem to be probable while they are false, or at any rate into believing them completely as though they were true.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: As many, therefore, as set out toward the perfection which is in Christ and toward the manner of life of the heavenly church, when they have heard the battles of the heresies, which do battle against the true faith and against one another in turn, and when they have heard the rumors of battles of "philosophy and vain seduction according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ", exercising themselves in the things that are said, seek and ponder the commandment of Christ who says: see, and they do indeed see the things that are said, but seeing lies dressed up with the appearance of truth, they are not led astray, but they hope, without any wound from such battles, to see the glorious coming of Christ, who is the word; especially if, hearing according to Christ's commandment of battles and rumors of battles, they suffer no disturbance of soul, but, protected under the peace of God which guards the "hearts and minds" of the worthy, they are not terrified.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if anyone, hearing of battles and rumors of battles, according to what we have expounded, is not attentive to see the things that are said in their various appearances of truth, and because he was not attentive to see is terrified, he will not only be deceived by the many who come in the name of Christ and say: I am Christ, but he will even be slain by swords of this kind, receiving incurable wounds — of which swords it is said: "swords do wound", whose wounds "the tongues of the wise" are wont to heal. But these who are disturbed and, because they do not look out for themselves, fall into a battle of this kind, are those who are wounded in the valley of Zion. and they die, of whom Scripture says: "your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead dead in battle", concerning whom it is fitting for us now only to give this indication.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But it is not for just any man to prepare himself to hear of wars and rumors of wars, so that hearing he may see and not be terrified, but for the man perfected in Christ, living indeed in the flesh yet not warring according to the flesh, whose weapons of warfare are not carnal but mighty toward God and able to destroy strongholds and the reasonings of those who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. For, according to Solomon, the many "fortified cities" of the heresies, fortified by the persuasion of words, "a wise man ascended," and ascending he "destroyed the fortification in which the impious trusted." Paul destroyed it, who had been prepared "for the destruction of fortified cities" set against the truth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Such a man, after he has heard of wars and rumors of wars, seeing and, as one wise, ascending upon the "fortified cities" and destroying the "fortifications in which the impious trusted," praising God and giving thanks to God (from whom he learned to fight such wars, and to keep the commandment which says: "sanctify war"), cries out and says: "Blessed be the Lord God, who teaches my hands for war, and my fingers for battle; my mercy and my refuge." And because of wars of this kind it is said of David by the wife of Nabal: "My lord will fight the wars of the Lord." And I think that these wars, which are read of in the Scriptures, are also mysteries of such battles; and that the destruction of those who fight against the congregation of the truth is likewise a mystery — especially those things which are read in the book of Joshua the son of Nun concerning the destructions of cities, and they are mysteries of all the congregations of the adversary powers.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Hearing, therefore, of wars and rumors of such wars, let us attend to what he says: see that you be not terrified. And we ought to know that it is necessary for these things to happen to one awaiting the coming of the Word, that he may hear wars and rumors of wars, but not immediately, as soon as he has heard, will the end be. For this reason every man who wishes to be saved must await the end, since "whoever shall persevere unto the end, this one shall be saved".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: According to Luke, however, if we hear of "wars and insurrections", let us not be troubled — the wars being those that arise from "knowledge falsely so named" and from the wisdom of "the princes of this world", and the insurrections being those of people who do not agree among themselves in the assembly of the church. For we plainly hear differing opinions about various matters (especially we who wish to advance toward that perfection which is in Christ) — not only wars outside the church, but also insurrections within the church itself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: From all these things the disciples of the apostles were strangers, of all of whom, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, "there was one heart and one soul"; for they had been confirmed "in the same mind and in the same knowledge". Yet let us, even if we hear of wars of this kind and insurrections of this sort, not be terrified.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For "these things must first come to pass", before we behold the perfection of the wisdom which is in Christ; "but the end" which we seek "shall not be at once". For we must be made stable and confirmed in peace, so that we may be without terror and not be troubled by insurrections, so that after these things we may be able to attain that end which lies not in the hearing of wars nor in the insurrections themselves; for the peaceful end is far removed from all these things.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: RABANUS.b Or, this is a warning to the Apostles not to flee from Jerusalem and Judæa in terror of these things, when they should begin to come upon them; because the end was not immediately, but the desolation of the province, and the destruction of the city and temple should not come till the fortieth year. And we know that most grievous woes, which spread over the whole province, fell out to the very letter.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: The final tribulation is preceded by many tribulations, and through the frequent evils that come before, the perpetual evils that will follow are indicated.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: And therefore after wars and seditions the end does not come immediately, because many evils must run before, so that they may be able to announce evil without end. But since so many signs of disturbance have been mentioned, we ought to touch briefly upon the consideration of each one, because it is necessary that we suffer some things from heaven, some from earth, some from the elements, some from men. For he says: "Nation will rise against nation"—behold the disturbance of men; "there will be great earthquakes in various places"—behold the look of wrath from above; "there will be pestilences"—behold the disorder of bodies; "there will be famine"—behold the barrenness of the earth.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: Because therefore all things are to be brought to an end, before the end all things are disturbed; and we who have sinned in all things are struck in all things.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: (Verses 7, 8.) For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there shall be pestilences and famines, and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginnings of sorrows. I do not doubt that these things indeed shall come to pass literally as they are written. But it seems to me that the kingdom against kingdom and their pestilence, whose speech spreads like cancer (2 Timothy 2), and the famine to hear the word of God, and the commotion of the whole earth, and the separation from true faith, are more understood in heretics who fight against each other, making victory for the Church. But what he said: These things, however, are the beginnings of sorrows, are better translated as birth pains, so that it may be understood as a kind of conception of the coming of the Antichrist, not as childbirth.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Figuratively; Kingdom rising against kingdom and pestilence of that discourse which spreadeth as a plague-spot, and hunger of hearing the word of God, and commotion throughout the earth, and separation from the true faith, my be rather understood of the heretics, who fighting among themselves give the victory to the Church.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But by "wars and rumors of wars," He meaneth, what I before said, the troubles coming upon them. After this, because, as I have already said, they supposed after that war the end would come, see how He warns them, saying, "But the end is not yet. For nation," He saith, "shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom." Of the preludes to the ills of the Jews doth He speak.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Then to show that He Himself also will assail the Jews with them, and war on them, He speaks not of battles only, but also of plagues sent from God, famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, showing that the wars also He Himself permitted to come upon them, and that these things do not happen for no purpose according to what has been before the accustomed course of things amongst men, but proceed from the wrath on high.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Therefore He saith, they shall come not by themselves or at once, but with signs. For that the Jews may not say, that they who then believed were the authors of these evils, therefore hath He told them also of the cause of their coming upon them. "For verily I say unto you," He said before, "all these things shall come upon this generation," having made mention of the stain of blood on them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Or otherwise; As the body sickens before the death of the man, so it must needs be that before the consummation of this world the earth should be shaken, as though it were palsied, with frequent earthquakes, the air should gather a deadly quality and become pestilential, and that the vital energy of the soil should fail, and its fruits wither. And by consequence of this scarcity, men are stirred up to robbery and war. But because war and strife arise sometimes from covctousness, and sometimes from desire of power and empty glory, of these which shall happen before the end of the world a yet deeper cause shall be assignable.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For as Christ's coming brought through His divine power peace to divers nations, so it shall be on the other hand, that when iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold, and God and His Christ shall desert them; wars shall be again when actions which beget wars are not hindered by holiness; and hostile powers when they are not restrained by the Saints and by Christ shall work unchecked in the hearts of men, stirring up nation against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if, as some will have it, famine and pestilence are from the Angels of Satan, these shall then gather might from opposite powers, when the salt of the earth, and the lights of the world, Christ's disciples, shall be no longer, destroying those things which the malice of dæmons hatches. Ofttimes in Israel famines and pestilences were caused by sin, and removed by the prayers of the Saints. (1 Kings 17:1. Jer. 14. James 5:17, 18.) Well is that said, In divers places, for God will not destroy the whole race of men at once, but judging them in portions, He gives opportunity of repentance.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if some stop be not put to these evils in their commencement, they will progress to worse, as it follows, These all are the beginnings of sorrows, that is, sorrows common to the whole world, and those which are to come upon the wicked who shall be tormented in most sharp pains.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For nation shall rise up against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there shall be famines and pestilences and earthquakes in various places; for all these are the beginnings of sorrows (24, 7. 8).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Mark has the same things, but adds "and tumults"; Luke likewise has these same things, but adds "and there shall be terrors from heaven and great signs and storms". Let us first expound the simple and bodily meaning of the passage.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For just as bodies fall sick before their death — the bodies, that is, of those who suffer no violence from outside — and just as in all cases it is through weakness that the way is made for separating the soul from its body, so also such and so great a creature as the world, when it has begun to be corrupted, as having, as it were, a beginning and an end (since "the things that are seen are temporal", and since "heaven and earth shall pass away"), must necessarily grow feeble before its corruption; so that the earth indeed is more frequently shaken and shattered by earthquakes, while the air, conceiving a certain disease-bearing force, becomes pestilential; and further still, the vital power of the earth, suddenly failing, chokes off the crops, and the generative power that produces every kind of tree, failing, chokes them off as well. Therefore, when these things happen, it follows that the movable nature also — being constituted, as it were, as some part of the whole world — must necessarily suffer along with the change of all things: for instance, not taking again its accustomed nourishment of foods, it comes to failure and is corrupted.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the heavens "shall perish", since "they shall grow old like a garment", and "whatever grows old and ages is near to destruction". It follows, then, that on account of the scarcity of foods men are stirred up to greed and to wars against those who do not suffer so great a scarcity; and that, by comparison with others who abound in the necessities of life, uprisings of some against others arise, and nation fights against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And it is possible that, together with the lack of other things, there should also come to be a lack of men possessing good sense, so that through this a tranquil and peaceful life is not found among many, but uprisings and quarrels and disturbances arise — sometimes indeed on account of greed, sometimes on account of the lust for rule, sometimes also on account of an insane craving for vainglory, and sometimes too through the desire for the vainglory of rulers, who are not content with their own kingdom, but wish to extend their own dominion and to subject many nations to themselves.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But someone will offer a still deeper explanation of the things that are to happen before the consummation of the world, and above all concerning the wars. For just as the coming of Christ made peace by divine power among very many nations — according to what the prophet says of him: "justice shall arise in his days, and abundance of peace until the moon be exalted" — and so the peace of the world was multiplied on account of the increases of the churches that were to come, in order that this peace might become an occasion of salvation for many, since they are not compelled to go out to wars and to fight for their homelands as formerly used to happen: so it follows also that, when on account of the abundance of iniquity "the love of many" has grown cold, and God and his Christ have for that reason forsaken them, wars come to pass once more — namely because the operations that sow wars are not prohibited by holiness, but are rather still further nourished on account of the ever-increasing malice of men — so that the cause of all the evils that befall is said to be those who did indeed come to the word, but afterward "all turned aside and together were made unprofitable" amid worldly evils.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For as long as the salt of the earth stands firm — those to whom the Lord said: "you are the salt of the earth" — all things hold together, seasoned by the salt; but after the salt itself has become tasteless, then (to speak according to the Scripture) the very things that were salted by it, being as it were unsalted, become insipid, are corrupted and stink and are dissolved.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And further, as long as the "light of the world" stands firm, all things are set aright, ordered by its clear illumination; but when this very light has been diminished in the souls of men — since it is not nourished by its proper and natural food — then, with darkness taking possession of all things, when all things have been brought into sorrow and calamities, there will come to be as it were an assembly of the adversary powers over all things, since they are not forbidden by the saints and by Christ in them, who used to forbid them, but as though in the darkness, without any prohibition, they will work in the hearts of men, so that they stir up nation against nation and kingdom against kingdom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if (as some are also pleased to hold) famines and pestilences too come about from operations of this kind and from the angels of Satan, then likewise famines and pestilences will at that time grow strong from the adversary powers, when the disciples of Christ are no longer the salt of the earth and the light of the world — they who are the princes of God's power, destroying in men the wars that the adversary powers make, and all the things that are sown from their malice.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And at one time indeed in Israel famines and pestilences used to come about on account of sins and droughts, which the prayers of the saints dissolved — those of Samuel, of Jeremiah, and of others like them. And it is well put: there shall be famines and pestilences and earthquakes in divers places.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For God does not will to destroy the human race all at once, but judging it by parts, little by little, while famines and pestilences and earthquakes come about in divers places, he grants a place for repentance to those who are amended by slight chastisements and are converted to God. And just as it is possible to bring medicinal aids to those who are beginning to fall ill, so, when famine and pestilences and earthquakes are beginning in divers places, it is possible to give to certain men purgative remedies toward the conduct and faith and wisdom of the saints.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if, when evils of this kind are beginning, no pious correction has been made, famines and pestilences and earthquakes will advance to worse, when the "abomination of desolation" has taken its place, not content with one part of the world: for it will come so that it may take its stand even "in the holy place".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Nevertheless the risings up of nations against nations and of kingdoms against kingdoms, and famines and pestilences and earthquakes in divers places continually arising, are said to be the beginnings of worse calamities, which the Lord called travail-pangs. If then such shall be the first-fruits of the pangs, what do you suppose the increases of the pangs will be? And what will the end also be of the general pangs in the whole world, so that they may exterminate not now by parts but the whole world?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria
