paragraphs.text: Yet I judge that the things which are to follow will be only against the impious, that they may be tortured with the sharpest and most prolonged pangs, until they lay down the seeds of sins which they have conceived and formed from the contrary operations. And Pharaoh indeed, desiring not to do well, commanded that every male whatsoever that should be born to the Hebrews be cast into the river; but God, being good, as one truly good, kills the seeds of evils which they have received, that through many labors and pains they may lay them down, since they conceived pain and brought forth iniquity. And what else befits God, save that he should kill every iniquity which sinners beget?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For such men the day of a death of this kind is better than the day of their own nativity, according to what is written: "better is the day of death than the day of nativity?" So too one will rightly say that a miscarriage is better than that which is born: "and I said the miscarriage is better than it; for" a miscarriage of this kind "comes in vanity and walks in darkness, and in darkness shall its name be covered". And these things we have treated more abundantly, looking to what follows, according to what he says: all these things are the beginnings of pangs.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Since I also consider there to be a moral sense in this passage too, according to what I have said, the following things must consequently be said here as well: that if anyone is to see the glorious and royal form of the Word and His glorious coming, it is necessary for him to be roused not only to hear "battles and reports" of intelligible "battles," so that, seeing, he may learn to be in no way terrified, but also to see the nation of some falsehood and the movement of words drawing men toward some sect rising up against some other nation of falsehood, since for nations of this kind there is never a peaceful end. This we frequently see happening among the heresies and among the churches of the malignant, when the nation of one heresy rises up against the nation of another heresy; so too the kingdom of some word will rise up against the kingdom of another erring word: since Satan and every falsehood is always divided against itself, and therefore cannot stand.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore he who sets out to see the glory of Christ and the kingdom—that is, the perfection of the Word and the kingdom that reigns and holds dominion, placing all adversary discourses under His feet and for the trampling of His feet—it is necessary for him, while seeking the truth, frequently to suffer a want of understandings, by which the soul is properly nourished for the searching out of the things that are to be sought. And just as at one time those who were journeying toward the land of promise were afflicted and suffered so great a hunger for carnal foods, that they might receive the heavenly manna, so must he who is to be nourished by the perfection of the Word be frequently tried by a want of understandings and yet suffer nothing from it. And we see this very thing daily in ourselves, when we seek some sense of truth in the Scriptures: before we find what we seek, we suffer a certain want of understandings, until such a want of understandings is dissolved in us by God, who gives to the worthy "food in due season" to eat and clothing to put on.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It is also necessary that he who sees the glorious coming—that is, the coming of wisdom into his soul—must see the pestilences of diseased discourses and suffer nothing from them. Now pestilent discourses are all those that are brought forth by pestilent men, who speak "iniquity on high" and set "their mouth in heaven" in pride and great presumption: for instance, the discourses of Marcion against the creator of the world and certain impious blasphemies are pestilences of souls, corrupting the minds of men and making souls sicken in the suspicions of errors; the fables of Valentinus too, about masculine and feminine ages, and about the birth of the creator of the world, which they have fabricated out of a false wisdom, and whatever other things they prattle—what else are these but pestilences; the discourses of Basilides also, which disparage those who strive even unto death for the truth so as to confess Jesus "before men," but teach that one may act indifferently in denying Him and in sacrificing to strange gods, pestilate no less and corrupt those who hear them, since in these same discourses they teach that there are no other punishments for sins except transmigrations of souls after death.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For, to pass over the fact that what is said is manifestly false, they further take away from men the salutary fear, and those who, even because of fear of future punishments, would have kept themselves from a multitude of sins, they nourish the boldness of their impiety. Many, therefore, will be the famines and pestilences for all who wish to see the glorious coming of Christ into their soul. But these will do them no harm; for they will only see them, and will suffer nothing from them. They will also suffer the movements of those things which are sought in very many places of the Scriptures that have an appearance of contradiction or of falsehoods; but afterward they will suffer nothing. Nor will the movement of false reports tear them away from the expectation of the glorious and divine and perfect coming of Jesus Christ the Word. And he who is to say: "from fear of You, O Lord, we conceived in the womb and were in travail, and we brought forth the spirit of salvation which You made upon the earth," or according to what has been said: "my children, of whom I am again in travail, until Christ be formed in you," must first of all come to be, amid all these pains, in famine and pestilences and movements, which, enduring, he will bring forth what he has conceived and formed within himself—Christ the Word—so that he may say at His birth: "behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy," and "glory to God in the highest and peace upon the earth."
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Nation shall rise against nation, shows the disquietude of men's minds; pestilences, the affliction of their bodies; famines, the barrenness of the soil; earthquakes in dicers places, wrath from heaven above.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: These all are the beginnings of sorrows, is better understood of pains of labour, as it were the conception of the coming of Antichrist, and not of the birth.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "All these are the beginning of sorrows," that is, of those that befall them.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Seest thou in what a state things were then, and how manifold was the war? And this is the beginning, when each of the things to be effected most required quiet. In what state then were they? for nothing hinders us from resuming the same things again. The first war was that of the deceivers; "For there shall come," He saith, "false Christs and false prophets:" the second, that of the Romans, "For ye shall hear," He saith, "of wars:" the third, that which bringeth on the "famines:" the fourth, "the pestilences" and "the earthquakes:" the fifth, "they shall deliver you into afflictions:" the sixth, "ye shall be hated of all men:" the seventh, "They shall betray one another, and hate one another" (an intestine war doth He here make known); then, "false Christs," and false brethren; then, "the love of the most shall wax cold," which is the cause of all the ills.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Seest thou numberless kinds of war, new and strange? Yet nevertheless in the midst of these things, and much more (for with the intestine wars was mingled also that of kinsmen), the gospel prevailed over the whole earth. "For the gospel," He saith, "shall be preached in the whole world."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But because all these things come not from the injustice of the one striking but from the merit of the world that suffers, the deeds of wicked men are set forth first when it is said: "But before all these things they will lay their hands upon you and persecute you, and deliver you to synagogues, leading you before kings and governors for my name's sake." As if he were saying openly: First the hearts of men are disturbed, and afterward the elements, so that when the order of things is thrown into confusion, it may be shown from what retribution this comes.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: (V. 9.) Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake. The apostles are a representation of all believers, not that the apostles themselves will be found in physical form at that time.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "Then shall they deliver you up to be afflicted, and shall kill you."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: In good season did He introduce their ills, having a consolation from the common miseries; and not in this way only, but also by His adding, that it is "for my name's sake. For ye shall be hated," He saith, "of all men for my name's sake. Then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and many false Christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall deceive many. And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold; but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: This is the greater evil, when the war is intestine too, for there were many false brethren. Seest thou the war to be threefold? from the deceivers, from the enemies, from the false brethren. See Paul too lamenting over the same things, and saying, "Without were fightings, within were fears;" and, "perils among false brethren," and again, "For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: After this again, what is more grievous than all, they shall not have so much as the consolation from love. Then indicating, that these things will in no degree harm the noble and the firm, He saith, Fear not, neither be troubled. For if ye show forth the patience that becomes you, the dangers will not prevail over you. And it is a plain proof of this, that the word shall surely be preached everywhere in the world, so much shall ye be above the things that alarm you. For, that they may not say, how then shall we live? He said more, Ye shall both live and preach everywhere. Therefore He added moreover, "And this gospel shall be preached in the whole world for a witness to all nations, and then shall the end come," of the downfall of Jerusalem.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Morally; He who shall see that glorious second coming of the word of God into his soul, must needs suffer in proportion to the measure of his proficiency assaults of opposing influences, and Christ in him must be hated by all, not only by the nations literally understood, but by the nations of spiritual vices. And in such enquiries there will be few who shall reach the truth with any fulness, the more part shall be offended and fall therefrom, betraying and accusing one another because of their disagreement respecting doctrines, which shall give rise to a mutual hatred.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Also there shall be many setting forth unsound words concerning things to come, and interpreting the Prophets in a manner in which they ought not; these are the false Prophets who shall deceive many, and who shall cause to wax cold that fervour of love which was before in the simplicity of the faith. But he who can abide firmly in the Apostolic tradition, he shall be saved; and the Gospel being preached to the minds of all shall be for a testimony to all nations, that is, to all the unbelieving thoughts of the soul.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Then they will hand you over to tribulations and will kill you, and you will be hated by all the nations for my name's sake. And then many will be scandalized and will hand one another over and will hate one another; and many false prophets will rise up and will lead many astray; and because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold. But he who endures to the end, this one will be saved. And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Even without exposition the text is clear of itself, since Christ's disciples have frequently been handed over to tribulations and have been killed for the sake of the word and have been hated by the nations on account of Christ. But if anyone wishes to examine what he says, by all the nations, he will not find it sufficiently certain. For is the people of Christ hated by all the nations, even by those dwelling in the farthest parts of the earth? — unless perhaps here too someone should say that all is set down for many by way of exaggeration of the great number. But if you set before yourself what he says, then they will hand you over, you will find a difficulty.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For it was not after "nation had risen against nation and kingdom against kingdom", and after "famines and pestilences in various places", that they were then handed over to tribulations and killed and hated by all the nations for Christ's name's sake: for even before these things came to pass, Christians were handed over to tribulations and, giving testimony to the truth, were killed and were hated by the nations among whom they dwelt.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But against this difficulty, one who wishes to understand according to the words will answer that then most of all will Christians be handed over to tribulations as never before, then are they to be hated most of all by all the nations dwelling together with them as never before, and they will suffer all things for Christ's name's sake, when "nation shall rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there shall be famines and pestilences and earthquakes in various places".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For those who are in calamities love, as they examine the causes of these things, to find something to say. When therefore these things befall the world, it follows — men, as it were, forsaking the worship of the gods — that they say that on account of the multitude of Christians wars and famines and pestilences come to pass. For frequently the Gentiles, and whoever were wise in the things of the nations, blamed the Christians as the cause of famine, but they also referred the causes of pestilences to the Church of Christ. And we know too that among us an earthquake occurred in certain places, and that certain collapses of buildings took place, so that those who were impious, outside the faith, said the Christians were the cause of the earthquake — on account of which the churches also suffered persecutions and were burned — and not only so, but even those who seemed prudent would say such things in public, that on account of the Christians the gravest earthquakes come to pass.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But as for what is said, and you will be hated by all the nations for my name's sake, one will be able to save it thus. For never indeed have all the nations agreed together as one against the Christians; but when the things Christ foretold come to pass, then all, as it were, are to be set aflame by certain nations beginning to blame the Christians, so that then persecutions may arise no longer in part, as before, but generally everywhere against the people of God. Then it will come about that many are scandalized who seem to stand firm in the faith; and the one will hand over the other. And there will be hatred even among those very ones who seem faithful.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Then many false prophets will rise up, deceiving the multitude of the senseless; then also, charity growing cold not only among the unbelievers but even among the faithful themselves, the fervor of charity will grow cold from the many iniquities, so that few remain contending for the truth unto the end, who alone are also to be saved. And with matters established in this state, the Gospel, which before had not been preached in the whole world (for many not only of the barbarian nations but even of our own nations have not until now heard the word of Christianity) — then it will be preached, so that every nation may hear the Gospel proclamation and no one be left who has not heard. And then will be the end of the age.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if these things are so, we shall no longer be in ignorance about what he says, then they will hand you over, nor shall we suspect that what he says is false — and you will be hated by all the nations for my name's sake — saying that the truth of this word is not yet fulfilled, so long as what he says has not come to pass, then many will be scandalized and will hand one another over. For not yet have many betrayers been made out of the Church, and not yet have many false prophets arisen deceiving many. So too, they have not yet been hated by all the nations, even by those dwelling in the farthest parts of the earth, for Christ's name's sake; so too, the Gospel of the kingdom has not yet been preached in the whole world.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the Gospel is not reported to have been preached among all the Ethiopians, especially among those who are beyond the river, nor among the Seres nor among the Ariacin nor … have heard the word of Christianity. And what shall we say of the Britons or the Germans, who are around the Ocean, or among the barbarian Dacians and Sarmatians and Scythians, of whom very many have not yet heard the word of the Gospel, but are to hear it at the very consummation of the age? For consider what he says: and this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all the nations, and then will be the end. But if anyone wishes rashly to say that the Gospel of the kingdom has already been preached in the whole world as a testimony to all the nations, one will consequently be able to say to him that, as regards what he says, then will be the end, the end has already come — which to say is a mark of great rashness and of a man not understanding what Paul says to the Thessalonians in his second epistle, saying: "Let no one deceive you in any way (as though the day of the Lord were at hand); for unless the falling-away come first and the man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition (and the rest), the day of the Lord will not be".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: These things we have expounded according to the simple tradition. But if we ought, in accordance with what we have handed down morally above, to understand here too a moral treatment, we shall expound such things as these: that he who is to see, according to the glorious coming of the word of God, that coming into his own soul, must, according to the measure of his progress toward the perfection of the word, suffer ambushes from the contrary operations, like a great athlete, and, handed over into tribulations, be forsaken.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For "many are the tribulations of the righteous", and the more righteous anyone wishes to become, so much the more, walking as it were with resolve the narrow and tribulated way, does he run into tribulations and, tribulated, is killed to the world; and the more he advances toward a clearer vision of the word, so much the more (since Christ is found more perfect in him) will he be hated by all who hate Christ, not so much by all the nations according to the flesh as by the nations of spiritual wickednesses.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the very implanted manifestation of the properties of Christ in him, on account of which he is also called a Christian, makes him hated by all who have the spirit of the world, while he still strives more and more toward the perfection of Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But also, in discussions and questions, few will be untouched, attaining the truth more fully. But more will be scandalized and will fall away from it, becoming betrayers and accusers of one another on account of dissension over the doctrines of the truth, which not all are able to grasp: which will become the cause of their hating one another. And when questions of this kind come upon the greater number, many indeed there will be who do not soundly hand down the discourse concerning things to come and who interpret the prophets in a way that is not fitting, whom one will not sin in calling false prophets, deceiving many; but very few there will be who search out the truth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the false doctrines will not indeed loosen the strong man from his purpose of truth. Those, however, who are itching in the ear they will multiply, speaking for their delight iniquity contrary to the law. And the contrary words of the many teachers will do so much harm that they will even make the fervent love (which before had been in the simplicity of faith) grow cold, through a supposed comprehension of the divine mysteries and of the truth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But he who is able, seeing all these things, to abide in the first purpose of the apostolic tradition and of the ecclesiastical leading, this one will be saved, and thus the Gospel, having been preached into the souls of all, will be as a testimony to all the nations, that is, to all the unbelieving thoughts of all souls.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But how should the people of Christ be hated by the nations who dwelt in the uttermost parts of the earth? But one may perhaps say, that in this place all is put hyperbolically for many. But this that He says, Then shall they deliver you, presents some difficulty; for before these things the Christians were delivered to tribulation. To this it may be answered, that at that time the Christians shall be more delivered to tribulation than ever. And persons in any misfortune love to examine into the origin of them, and to talk about them. Hence when the worship of the Gods shall be almost deserted by reason of the multitude of Christians, it will be said that that is the cause of the wars, and famines, and pestilences; and of the earthquakes also they will say that the Christians are the cause, whence the persecution of the Churches.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And that, Ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake, might be then applied thus; That indeed at this time all nations are conspired together against the Christians, but that when the things foretold by Christ shall have come to pass, then there shall be persecutions, not as before in places, but every where against the people of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For what desert so many evils are to be brought upon Jerusalem, and the whole Jewish province the Lord shows, when He adds, Then shall they deliver you up,&c.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: "Then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and many false Christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall deceive many."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: This is the greater evil, when the war is intestine too, for there were many false brethren. Seest thou the war to be threefold? from the deceivers, from the enemies, from the false brethren. See Paul too lamenting over the same things, and saying, "Without were fightings, within were fears;" and, "perils among false brethren," and again, "For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But the whole passage might be referred to the end of the world. For then shall many be offended, and depart from the faith, when they see the numbers and wealth of the wicked, and the miracles of Antichrist, and they shall persecute their brethren; and Antichrist shall send false Prophets, who shall deceive many; iniquity shall abound, because the number of the wicked shall be increased; and love shall wax cold, because the number of the good shall diminish.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: Such was Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons, who led astray many by his pretences. And Simon Magus who, armed with diabolic works and words, perverted many by false miracles.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: The fact that there are such men confessing themselves to be Christians, and admitting the crucified Jesus to be both Lord and Christ, yet not teaching His doctrines, but those of the spirits of error, causes us who are disciples of the true and pure doctrine of Jesus Christ, to be more faithful and stedfast in the hope announced by Him. For what things He predicted would take place in His name, these we do see being actually accomplished in our sight.
paragraphs.author: Justin Martyr

paragraphs.text: For he said, "Many shall come in My name, clothed outwardly in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves." And, "There shall be schisms and heresies." And, "Beware of false prophets, who shall come to you clothed outwardly in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves." And, "Many false Christs and false apostles shall arise, and shall deceive many of the faithful." There are, therefore, and there were many, my friends, who, coming forward in the name of Jesus, taught both to speak and act impious and blasphemous things; and these are called by us after the name of the men from whom each doctrine and opinion had its origin.
paragraphs.author: Justin Martyr

paragraphs.text: As the capture of Jerusalem approached, many rose up, calling themselves Christians, and deceived many; such Paul calls false brethren, John Antichrists.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: (Verse 12, 13.) And since iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold. But he who perseveres to the end, he will be saved. He did not deny the faith of all, but of many. For many are called, but few are chosen. For in the apostles and those like them, charity will remain, of which it is written: 'Many waters cannot quench love' (Song of Solomon 8:7). And even Paul himself said: 'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?' tribulation, or distress, or famine (Rom. VIII, 35)? and so on.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Observe, He says, the love of many, (Rom. 8:35.) not 'of all,' for in the Apostles, and those like them, love would continue, as Paul speaks, Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: "And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold; but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: After this again, what is more grievous than all, they shall not have so much as the consolation from love. Then indicating, that these things will in no degree harm the noble and the firm, He saith, Fear not, neither be troubled. For if ye show forth the patience that becomes you, the dangers will not prevail over you.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: And if thou art minded to learn these things more distinctly, I mean, the famines, the pestilences, the earthquakes, the other calamities, peruse the history about these things composed by Josephus, and thou wilt know all accurately. Therefore Himself too said, "Be not troubled, for all must be;" and, "He that endureth to the end, the same shall be saved;" and, "The gospel shall surely be preached in all the world." For when weakened and faint at the fear of what had been said, He braces them up by saying, Though ten thousand things be done, the gospel must be preached in every part of the world, and then shall the end come.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: That is, true love towards God and our neighbour, in proportion as each surrenders himself to iniquity, in that proportion will the flame of charity in his heart be extinguished.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: But as the conquering power of things evil is on the increase-which is the characteristic of the last times -things good are now not allowed either to be born, so corrupted are the seminal principles; or to be trained, so deserted are studies; nor to be enforced, so dined are the laws.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: "In your patience you shall possess your souls." The possession of the soul is placed in the virtue of patience because patience is the root and guardian of all virtues. Through patience we truly possess our souls, because while we learn to master ourselves, we begin to possess that very thing which we are.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: Patience, however, is to endure the evils of others with equanimity, and to feel no sting of resentment even against the one who inflicts the evils. For whoever bears the evils of a neighbor in such a way that he nevertheless grieves silently and seeks an opportunity for fitting retribution does not display patience but merely shows it outwardly. For it is written: "Love is patient, love is kind." It is patient so as to bear the evils of others, and kind so as to love even those whom it bears. Hence Truth says through Himself: "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who persecute and slander you." It is therefore a virtue before men to tolerate adversaries, but the virtue before God is to love them, because God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before His eyes on the altar of good works.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: For Solomon indicates how great is the height at which the virtue of patience excels, saying: "The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities." It is therefore a lesser victory to capture cities, because what is conquered is external. But what is conquered through patience is greater, because the mind is overcome by itself, and it subjects itself to itself, when patience prostrates it in the humility of forbearance.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: Whoso shall endure unto the end, i. e. to the end of his life; for whoso to the end of his life shall persevere in the confession of the name of Christ, and in love, he shall be saved.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: But "by patience," says He, "ye shall yourselves be saved." Of this very patience the Psalm says, "The patient endurance of the just shall not perish for ever; " because it is said in another Psalm, "Precious (in the sight of the Lord) is the death of the just"-arising, no doubt, out of their patient endurance, so that Zechariah declares: "A crown shall be to them that endure.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: To speak plainly, if they who reproach us with harshness, or esteem heresy (to exist) in this (our) cause, foster the "infirmity of the flesh" to such a degree as to think it must have support accorded to it in frequency of marriage; why do they in another case neither accord it support nor foster it with indulgence-when, (namely), torments have reduced it to a denial (of the faith)? For, of course, that (infirmity) is more capable of excuse which has fallen in battle, than (that) which (has fallen) in the bed-chamber; (that) which has succumbed on the rack, than (that) which (has succumbed) on the bridal bed; (that) which has yielded to cruelty, than (that) which (has yielded) to appetite; that which has been overcome groaning, than (that) which (has been overcome) in heat. But the former they excommunicate, because it has not "endured unto the end: " the latter they prop up, as if withal it has "endured unto the end.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: (Ep. 199, 46.) But that this preaching the Gospel of the kingdom in all the world was accomplished by the Apostles, we have not any certain evidence, to prove. There are numberless barbarous nations in Africa, among whom the Gospel is not even yet preached, as it is easy to learn from the prisoners who are brought from thence. But it cannot be said that these have no part in the promise of God. For God promised with an oath not the Romans only, but all nations to the seed of Abraham.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: But in whatever nation there is yet no Church established, it must needs be that there should be one, not that all the people should believe; for how then should that be fulfilled, Ye shall be hated of all nations for my name's sake, unless there be in all nations those who hate and those; who are hated? That preaching therefore was not accomplished by the Apostles, while as yet there were nations among whom it had not begun to be fulfilled. The words of the Apostle also, Their sound hath gone out into all the world, though expressed as of time past, are meant to apply to something future, not yet completed; as the Prophet, whose words he quotes, said that the Gospel bore fruit and grew in the whole world (Ps. 19:4.), to show thereby to what extent its growth should come. If then we know not when it shall be that the whole world shall be filled with the Gospel, undoubtedly we know not when the end shall be; but it shall not be before such time.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: The Gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world: and along with it shall the woman too be told of who did him a kindness—and we see that all these predictions have been fulfilled. For the Christians who were at one time persecuted by the Greeks and Jews have conquered, and drawn their persecutors over to their own side. In like manner we see that the Church has never been destroyed, but that its adherents have been greatly multiplied, and that similarly the whole earth has been filled with the doctrine of the Lord Christ, and is still being filled, and that the gospel is preached throughout all the world. This I avouch to be the veritable fact, from what I have seen and heard in the many places which I have visited.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: Even in Taprobanê, an island in Further India, where the Indian sea is, there is a Church of Christians, with clergy and a body of believers, but I know not whether there be any Christians in the parts beyond it. In the country called Malê, where the pepper grows, there is also a church, and at another place called Calliana there is moreover a bishop, who is appointed from Persia.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: In the island, again, called the Island of Dioscoridês, which is situated in the same Indian sea, and where the inhabitants speak Greek, having been originally colonists sent thither by the Ptolemies who succeeded Alexander the Macedonian, there are clergy who receive their ordination in Persia, and are sent on to the island, and there is also a multitude of Christians. I sailed along the coast of this island, but did not land upon it. I met, however, with some of its Greek-speaking people who had come over into Ethiopia.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: And so likewise among the Bactrians and Huns and Persians, and the rest of the Indians, Persarmenians, and Medes and Elamites, and throughout the whole land of Persia there is no limit to the number of churches with bishops and very large communities of Christian people, as well as many martyrs, and monks also living as hermits.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: So too in Ethiopia and Axôm, and in all the country about it; among the people of Happy Arabia—who are now called Homerites—through all Arabia and Palestine, Phoenicia, and all Syria and Antioch as far as Mesopotamia; among the Nubians and the Garamantes, in Egypt, Libya, Pentapolis, Africa and Mauretania, as far as southern Gadeira, there are everywhere churches of the Christians, and bishops, martyrs, monks and recluses, where the Gospel of Christ is proclaimed.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: So likewise again in Cilicia, Asia, Cappadocia, Lazica and Pontus, and in the northern countries occupied by the Scythians, Hyrcanians, Heruli, Bulgarians, Greeks and Illyrians, Dalmatians, Goths, Spaniards, Romans, Franks, and other nations, as far as Gadeira on the ocean towards the northern parts, there are believers and preachers of the Gospel confessing the resurrection from the dead; and so we see the prophecies being fulfilled over the whole world.
paragraphs.author: Cosmas Indicopleustes

paragraphs.text: (Verse 14) And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world, as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come. The sign of the Lord's coming is the preaching of the Gospel in the whole world, so that no one may be without excuse; which has either already been fulfilled, or is about to be fulfilled very soon. For I do not think that any nation remains which does not know the name of Christ. And although it may not have had preachers, it cannot ignore the expectation of faith from neighboring nations.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And the sign of the Lord's second coming is, that the Gospel shall be preached in all the world, so that all may be without excuse.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: This, we may observe, He saith elsewhere also; "This gospel shall be preached in all the world for a testimony to all the nations, and then shall the end come;" to the nations, to them that obey not, to them that believe not. Thus, lest any one should say, "And wherefore preach to all, if all are not to believe?"-it is that I may be found to have done all my own part, and that no man may hereafter be able to find fault, as though he had not heard. For the very preaching shall bear witness against them, and they will not be able hereafter to say, "We heard not;" for the word of godliness "hath gone out unto the ends of the world."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 25

paragraphs.text: For in proof that He meant this, and that before the taking of Jerusalem the gospel was preached, hear what Paul saith, "Their sound went into all the earth;" and again, "The gospel which was preached to every creature which is under Heaven." And seest thou him running from Jerusalem unto Spain? And if one took so large a portion, consider what the rest also wrought. For writing to others also, Paul again saith concerning the gospel, that "it is bringing forth fruit, and growing up in every creature which is under Heaven."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But what meaneth, "For a witness to all nations?" Forasmuch as though it was everywhere preached, yet it was not everywhere believed. It was for a witness, He saith, to them that were disbelieving, that is, for conviction, for accusation, for a testimony; for they that believed will bear witness against them that believed not, and will condemn them. And for this cause, after the gospel is preached in every part of the world, Jerusalem is destroyed, that they may not have so much as a shadow of an excuse for their perverseness. For they that saw His power shine throughout every place, and in an instant take the world captive, what excuse could they then have for continuing in the same perverseness? For in proof that it was everywhere preached at that time, hear what Paul saith, "of the gospel which was preached to every creature which is under Heaven."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Which also is a very great sign of Christ's power, that in twenty or at most thirty years the word had reached the ends of the world. "After this therefore," saith He, "shall come the end of Jerusalem." For that He intimates this was manifested by what follows.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: When every nation shall have heard the preaching of the Gospel, then shall come the end of the world. For at this time there are many nations, not of barbarians only, but of our own, who have not yet heard the word of Christianity.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Morally; He who shall see that glorious second coming of the word of God into his soul, must needs suffer in proportion to the measure of his proficiency assaults of opposing influences, and Christ in him must be hated by all, not only by the nations literally understood, but by the nations of spiritual vices. And in such enquiries there will be few who shall reach the truth with any fulness, the more part shall be offended and fall therefrom, betraying and accusing one another because of their disagreement respecting doctrines, which shall give rise to a mutual hatred.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Also there shall be many setting forth unsound words concerning things to come, and interpreting the Prophets in a manner in which they ought not; these are the false Prophets who shall deceive many, and who shall cause to wax cold that fervour of love which was before in the simplicity of the faith. But he who can abide firmly in the Apostolic tradition, he shall be saved; and the Gospel being preached to the minds of all shall be for a testimony to all nations, that is, to all the unbelieving thoughts of the soul.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the Lord knew that the hearts of the disciples would be made sad by the destruction of Jerusalem, and overthrow of their nation, and He therefore comforts them with a promise that more of the Gentiles should believe than of the Jews should perish.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: (Ep. 199. 31.) Luke, in order to show that the abomination of desolation foretold by Daniel had reference to the time of the siege of Jerusalem, repeats these words of our Lord, When ye shall see Jerusalem encompassed by armies, then know ye that its desolation draweth nigh. (Luke 21:20.)
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: (ubi sup.) For let us not suppose that the computation of Daniel's weeks was interfered with by this shortening of those days, or that they were not already at that time complete, but had to be completed afterwards in the end of all things, for Luke most plainly testifies that the prophecy of Daniel was accomplished at the time when Jerusalem was overthrown.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: Or otherwise; It is a sign of His future coming that the Lord gives, when He says, When ye shall see the abomination. For the Prophet spoke this of the times of Antichrist; and he calls abomination that which coming against God claims to itself the honour of God. It is the abomination of desolation, because it will desolate the earth with wars and slaughter; and it is admitted by the Jews, and set up in the holy place, that where God had been invoked by the prayers of the saints, into that same place admitted by the unbelievers it might be adored with the worship of God. And because this error will be peculiar to the Jews, that having rejected the truth they should adopt a lie, He warns them to leave Judæa, and flee to the mountains, that no pollution or infection might be gathered by admixture with a people who should believe on Antichrist.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 15.) When therefore you shall see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place: he that readeth, let him understand. When we are called to understanding, it is shown to be a mystical happening. We read in Daniel in this way: And in the middle of the week, sacrifice and oblation shall be taken away: and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation: and the desolation shall continue even to the consummation, and to the end. The apostle speaks about this (II Thess.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: II): that the man of sin and the adversary will be exalted against everything that is called God and worshiped, so that he dares to stand in the temple of God and show himself to be God, whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with all power, signs, and lying wonders, and destroys those who do not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved. It can be understood either simply or of the Antichrist, or of the image of Caesar, which Pilate placed in the temple, or of the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which stood in the holy of holies until the present day. Abominatio quoque, secundum veterem Scripturam, idolum nuncupatur; et idcirco additur, desolationis; quod in desolato templo atque destructo idolum positum sit.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: That, Let him that readeth understand, is said to call us to the mystic understanding of the place. What we read in Daniel is this; And in the midst of the week the sacrifice and the oblation shall be taken away, and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolations until the consummation of the time, and consummation shall be given upon the desolate. (Dan. 9:27. sec. LXX.)
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Or it may be understood of the statue of Cæsar, which Pilate set up in the temple; or of the equestrian statue of Adrian, which stood to the present time in the very Holy of Holies. For, according to the Old Scripture, an idol is called 'abomination;' of desolation is added, because the idol was set up in the desolated and deserted temple.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Observe this economy of the Holy Spirit in this, that John wrote nothing of all this, that he might not seem to be writing a history after the event; for he survived sometime the taking of Jerusalem. But these who died before it, and saw nothing of it, these write it, that the power of prophecy may shine manifestly forth.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Whence one may most marvel at Christ's power, and their courage, for that they preached in such times, in which most especially the Jewish state was warred against, in which most especially men regarded them as movers of sedition, when Caesar commanded all of them to be driven away. And the result was the same as if any one (when the sea was stirred up on every side, and darkness was filling all the air, and successive shipwrecks taking place, and when all their fellow-sailors were at strife above, and monsters were rising up from beneath, and with the waves devouring the mariners, and thunderbolts falling, and their being pirates, and those in the vessel plotting one against another), were to command men inexperienced in sailing, and who had not so much as seen the sea to sit at the rudder, and to guide and fight the vessel, and when an immense fleet was coming against them with a great array, making use of a single bark, with her crew in this disturbed state, to sink and subdue the fleet.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: For indeed by the heathens they were hated as Jews, and by the Jews were stoned, as waging war against their laws; and nowhere could they stand.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Thus were all things, precipices, and reefs, and rocks, the things in the cities, the things in the fields, the things in the houses, and every single person was at war with them; generals and rulers, and private persons, and all nations, and all people, and a turmoil which cannot be set forth by words. For the Jewish race was exceedingly detestable to the government of the Romans, as having occasioned them endless trouble; and not even from this did the preaching of the word take hurt; but the city was stormed and set on fire, and involved its inhabitants in countless evils; but the apostles that came from thence, introducing new laws, prevailed even over the Romans.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: O strange and wonderful facts! Countless myriads of Jews did the Romans then subdue, and they did not prevail over twelve men fighting against them naked and unarmed. What language can set forth this miracle? For they that teach need to have these two things, to be worthy of credit, and to be beloved by them whom they are instructing; and together with these, and besides them, that their sayings should be easy of reception, and the time should be free from trouble and tumults.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But then were all the contraries to these. For while they did not seem worthy of credit, they were withdrawing from such as did seem worthy of it, those who had been deceived by them. So far from being loved, they were even hated, and were taking men away from what they loved, both habits, and hereditary customs, and laws.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Again, their injunctions had great difficulty; but the things, from which they were withdrawing men, much pleasure. And many were the perils, many the deaths, both themselves and they that obeyed them underwent, and together with all this, the time also occasioned them much difficulty, teeming with wars, tumults, disturbance, so that, even if there had been none of the things we have mentioned, it would have quite thrown all things into confusion.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: We have good occasion to say, "Who shall tell the mighty works of the Lord, and make all His praises to be heard." For if his own people amid signs hearkened not to Moses, because of the clay only, and the bricks; who persuaded these that every day were beaten and slain, and were suffering incurable evils, to leave a quiet life, and to prefer thereto this which was teeming with blood and death, and that when they who preached it were strangers to them, and very hostile in every way? For I say not unto nations and cities and people, but into a small house let one bring in him that is hated of all that are in the house, and by him endeavor to bring them away from those whom they love, from father, and wife, and child, will he not surely be seen torn in pieces, before he hath opened his mouth?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: And if there be added moreover a tumult and strife of husband and wife in the house, will they not stone him to death before he steps on the threshold? And if he also be one whom they may readily despise, and who enjoins galling things, and commands them who are living in luxury to practise self restraint, and together with this the conflict be against those who are far more in numbers and who excel him, is it not quite manifest that he will be utterly destroyed?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: Yet nevertheless, this, which is impossible to be done in one house, this hath Christ accomplished in all the world, through precipices and furnaces, and ravines, and rocks, and land and sea at war with Him, bringing in the healers of the world.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: For He brought in also a prophecy, to confirm their desolation, saying, "But when ye shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place, let him that readeth understand." He referred them to Daniel. And by "abomination" He meaneth the statue of him who then took the city, which he who desolated the city and the temple placed within the temple, wherefore Christ calleth it, "of desolation." Moreover, in order that they might learn that these things will be while some of them are alive, therefore He said, "When ye see the abomination of desolation."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 75

paragraphs.text: But if it is necessary, for the sake of those who wish and are able to ascend by the word to loftier things, let us take up again from the beginning the words of the Gospel set forth, and, so far as we can, let us expound the same once more spiritually.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And first let us take up the word about the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place. For he who reads must be diligent and understanding, so that he not be led astray by the abomination of desolation. The holy place, then, understood spiritually, is every utterance of divine Scripture which the holy prophets who were from the beginning spoke — Moses and, after him, the rest; and not only they, but also the utterance of the evangelists and apostles of Jesus Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: In this holy place, then, of all the Scriptures, both of the Old Testament and of the New, the Antichrist, which is the false word, has frequently stood, showing himself — through this very fact that he seems to stand in the divine Scriptures — as though he were God and as though he himself were Christ the Word of God; and he himself is the abomination of desolation. For one may frequently see, in the impious argumentations of doctrines among the heresies, this abomination of desolation, that is, the Antichrist, the false word, the abomination that desolates of God every man who has received into himself that abomination opposing the truth, exalting itself above every word that is outside it which is announced to be the word of God, exalting itself also above everything that any one of men wishes to worship, whether truly or falsely (for each doctrine of the heresies is not only opposed to the truth, but also to the other doctrines that are likewise false); and since it is so exalted that it even sits in the temple of the Scriptures, through that very temple, that is, through the Scriptures themselves, it wishes to show itself to be truly God the Word.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Always, therefore, let him who reads the divine Scriptures understand them, most of all when he shall have seen the abomination of desolation (according to the things we have said) standing in that holy place which we have expounded, of the holy Scriptures. But he who has understood it will destroy it by the true tradition, that is, by the "illumination of the coming" of Christ who is the truth — that word which seems to stand in another's holy place; and, understanding such an abomination of desolation, he will render it void, and will cast it out from the holy place in which it seems to stand. But most of all will Christ destroy it, who speaks in him, the true light. And this Christ, if he speaks in someone who is willing to hear and to be profited, is not weakened, but every false word, which is the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place and sitting in the temple of God (which is the Antichrist), he "will slay with the spirit of his mouth" through those who have offered themselves as capable of him. And that false word frequently does not merely stand, but even sits in the temple, when it seems to be constructed as if reasonably and well. But those who see this abomination of desolation, so that they can say concerning it: "for we are not ignorant of its cunning", understanding therein while they read the things that are true, let them flee the false, and let them withdraw where falsehood will not be able to seize them.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But falsehood cannot seize those who flee from the Judea of the letter to the spiritual and intelligible things and the sublime mountains of truth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And that we may understand let them flee into the mountains, take as an example what is said manifestly of a praiseworthy flight, such as what the Apostle says: "flee fornication", and what Wisdom says: "as from the face of a serpent, flee sin", or such as what Rebecca says to Jacob in a mystery: "behold, Esau thy brother threatens to kill thee. Now therefore, my son, hear my voice, and rising up flee to Laban my brother in Haran; and dwell with him some days, until the wrath of thy brother be turned away". And everyone (I think) who is a son of Jacob, completing the works of Jacob, understanding every disposition hateful to God, which is Esau, flees as one who understands.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if he does not flee it, he is a fornicator and defiled like Esau, and, as one not fleeing Esau but dwelling together with him, he does not become a son of Jacob, who had fled it. But Jacob himself, dwelling with Laban usefully for himself and for the dispensation which was according to God, "hid the heart of the Syrian, so that he did not announce to him that he was fleeing", and he himself was fleeing "and all that was his". It is good, therefore, to flee even from Laban, from the counselor of carnal qualities, in which one who dwells ought not to remain, but to flee with his whole household.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For even if he should wish to pursue after him, God will turn him away from those fleeing him, so that, even if he should afterward at some time seize him, he can do him no evil while he confidently declares and says: "with whomsoever thou shalt find thy gods, let him not live in the sight of our brethren: recognize what of thine is with me, and take it"; for nothing can be recognized among Jacob of the things of Laban.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: In these Gospel sayings, then, which we are treating in the present, it is commanded that those who recognize the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place should understand therein while they read, so that they may flee into the mountains. He, therefore, who is held established in such a Judea as we have spoken of, that is, "in the oldness of the letter", let him flee into the mountains of spiritual newnesses.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if anyone be found to have ascended upon the housetop of the word and to stand upon the summit of its edifice, let him not come down thence on the occasion of taking anything out of his house; for he will have no need, remaining on the housetop and restraining himself lest ever he come down thence.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if anyone be in the field — whether in that in which a treasure is hidden, as the Lord says in a certain parable, or such as was that full field of Jacob, to which his father, blessing him, had likened him, saying: "behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord hath blessed", in which field, according to the spiritual blessings of the law, everyone is blessed who has lived according to the law, as the Scripture says: "blessed art thou in the city, and blessed art thou in the field" — he, therefore, who is in such a field of the whole planting "which the heavenly Father planted", let him not return back. For not only is that man "who puts his hand to the plough and has turned back, not fit for the kingdom of God", but also he who is in the field which we have handed down, and has turned back for the sake of the things which he ought to have forgotten, will without doubt fall into the abomination of desolation, that is, into the seduction of the lying word: and most of all if he has stripped himself of his old garment, that is, of "the old man with his deeds", and has again turned back to take his garment.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Diligently, therefore, ought we to attend, lest perchance we should wish, descending, to take any of those things which are below and are in the house, or, leaving the field and turned back, to seek again the garment left behind — when we ought "to reach for the things that are before, and to forget the things that are behind", and neither to stand in any of that region, but to be saved on the mountain, so that we be not seized together with those who were burned up because they were caught in Sodom.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Mystically; In the holy place of the Scriptures, both Old and New Testament, Antichrist, that is, false word, has often stood; let those who see this flee from the Judæa of the letter to the high mountains of truth. And whoso has been found to have gone up to the house-top of the word, and to be standing upon its summit, let him not come down thence as though he would fetch any thing out of his house.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if he be in the field in which the treasure is hid, and return thence to his house, he will run into the temptation of a false word; but especially if he have stripped off his old garment, that is, the old man, and should have returned again to take it up. Then the soul, as it were with child by the word, not having yet brought forth, is liable to a woe; for it casts that which it had conceived, and loses that hope which is in the acts of truth; and the same also if the word has been brought forth perfect and entire, but not having yet attained sufficient growth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Let them that flee to the mountains pray that their flight be not in the winter or on the sabbath-day, because in the serenity of a settled spirit they may reach the way of salvation, but if the winter overtake them they fall amongst those whom they would fly from. And there be some who rest from evil works, but do not good works; be your flight then not on such sabbath when a man rests from good works, for no man is easily overcome in times of peril from false doctrines, except he is unprovided with good works. But what sorer affliction is there than to see our brethren deceived, and to feel one's self shaken and terrified?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Those days mean the precepts and dogmas of truth; and all interpretations coming of science falsely so called (1 Tim. 6:20.) are so many additions to those days, which God shortens by those whom He wills.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But now let us set forth the very text of the Gospel. We have said that the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place is the general who surrounded Jerusalem with his army. And so, since the worst of things befell those who were then in Judea, therefore, prophesying that these things would come to pass, the Lord says to the people: then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. And such were the things that befell in that time — so to speak — that whoever was upon the roof of the house had no time to come down and take anything out of his house, and he who was in the field could not return to the city and take his garment.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And there was then no time for mercy, neither upon those with child nor upon those giving suck nor upon their infants; therefore he says (I speak with respect to the words): "woe to those who are with child and to those who are nursing in those days". And as though speaking to the Jews, who supposed that on the Sabbath one ought neither to do work nor to walk a road farther than is a Sabbath's journey, therefore he says: "but pray that your flight be not in winter or on the Sabbath"; for not only on the "Sabbath", but also in "winter" it was a most grievous thing to seek safety through flight.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Moreover, it is reported by those who wrote down the Jewish history concerning the things that then befell, that "great tribulation" came upon the people "such as never was from the beginning of the world unto" the time of Christ. But neither afterward can it come to pass that such things befall them, because they dared to lay hands upon the true Christ of God, whose mystery and name David venerated when he said concerning Saul, who was persecuting him and wishing to kill him: "I will not lay my hands upon the Lord's anointed".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And by the cutting short of those days that was to come "for the sake of the elect" of God who believe in Christ, we understand a shortening of those days. But then, when the people were set in great calamity and the elect who are in Judea were suffering perils, many seducers were saying: "behold, here is Christ, behold, there". Teaching his disciples to be on guard against them, he said: "then if anyone shall say to you: behold, here is Christ, behold, there, do not believe; for false christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall give great signs and wonders".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And one may name either Simon Magus, who said that he was the great power of God, or anyone who was like him, wishing "to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect". These things we have set forth by way of anticipation, adding in this place no other exposition than the one that is according to the text, for the sake of those who take delight in a simple tradition, so that we might say the things that seem useful to them, since the Lord, prophesying that these things would come to pass, foreknowing the truth, expounded them.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: When you see the abomination of desolation, which was written of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place, let him who reads understand.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The words of the prophet which he spoke concerning the abomination of desolation that was to come are these: "and he shall confirm the covenant to many for one week, and in the middle of the week the sacrifice and the offering shall be taken away, and upon the temple there shall be an abomination of desolation, and even unto the consummation of the time the consummation shall be given upon the desolation".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Truly indeed to grasp the sayings of Daniel belongs to no other than the Holy Spirit who was in Daniel, so as to make plain the whole discourse concerning the weeks and concerning the abomination of desolation spoken by him. But if it behooves us also to set forth a few things, according to what seems good to us, about this passage, it must be said that the discourse seems to indicate the seventy years which were after the coming of our Savior.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For this week, which because of the seven decades of years is called a week, confirmed the covenant to many, when the apostles of Christ also, after his ascension, being intent upon prayer and the word, were illumined by God into all knowledge of the will of the divine Scriptures by the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But in the middle of the week, that is, in three and a half decades of years, the sacrifice of the altar was taken away, that is, in thirty-five years was fulfilled what had been written: "in the middle of the week the sacrifice and the offering shall be taken away". And then also upon the temple which was in Jerusalem was made the abomination of the desolation of the temple and of the city, namely at that time "when they saw Jerusalem surrounded by an army", so that (according to what the Savior had prophesied concerning it) they might recognize "that its desolation had drawn near". And this abomination of desolation made upon the temple by the army surrounding Jerusalem, the prophet says remains "until the time of consummation", so that the consummation of the world may come upon the desolation of Jerusalem and of the temple which is in it. And where are they "who say they are Jews and are not"? who say: The Jerusalem which is below shall be built, before the consummation of the age comes to pass? "The consummation", he says, "shall be given upon its desolation".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if the temple shall also be built, it shall be built for him "who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or that is worshiped, so that he sits in a temple" of this kind, "showing himself as though he were God": "whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of his mouth and shall destroy with the illumination of his coming". Whether therefore it pleases some that this Jerusalem be built upon the earth, nevertheless it will not be false which is said, that the consummation is to be given "upon its own desolation".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if it behooves us also to say something about the times, we say that in the Chronicles of a certain Phlegon it is said (if however we ought to accept even this man as speaking truly about the temple) that around the fortieth year from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar the destruction of Jerusalem and of the temple which was in it took place.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Deduct therefore about three years of the Lord's preaching and the time of his resurrection, when "appearing to them for forty days" he taught "them concerning the kingdom of God", and you will find perhaps more or less that around the middle of the "week" (reckoning by decades of years) was fulfilled what was said: "my sacrifice and offering shall be taken away", when also "upon the temple the abomination of desolation" was made, which desolation will remain until the time of consummation; for the "consummation", according to what we have said, "shall be given upon the desolation".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if such a tradition of the "week" is established for us, we saying (as far as concerns the saying) that there has been fulfilled what was said, not only: "my sacrifice and offering shall be taken away", but also that which is written, that the abomination of desolations should befall upon the temple, then without doubt the coming of Christ is manifestly shown even from the words of Daniel the prophet saying: "seventy weeks are cut short upon your people and upon the holy city, that sin may be consummated and sin be sealed and iniquities be blotted out, and that eternal justice may be brought in, and that vision and prophet may be sealed, and the holy of holies be anointed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And you shall know and understand: from the going forth of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem unto Christ the leader there are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and it shall be turned back and the street and wall shall be rebuilt, and the times shall be emptied out. And after sixty-two weeks the anointing shall perish and judgment is not in it; but the city and the sanctuary he shall corrupt with the leader who comes, and they shall be cut off in a flood; and even unto the end of the war there is a cutting-off of destruction.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And he shall confirm the covenant to many for one week; and in the middle of the week my sacrifice and offering shall be taken away, and the pinnacles, from the destruction unto the consummation of the haste". After these things follows the discourse which we have expounded, running thus: "and he shall confirm the covenant to many for one week" and the rest.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I think that the seventy weeks cut short "upon the people and upon the holy city, that sin may be consummated" are four thousand nine hundred years from Adam unto the seventy years which were after the dispensation of Christ. For the sin of the people was consummated, on account of which it was also forsaken by God. And their sin indeed was sealed. But the injustice of believers was blotted out, and after its blotting out eternal life was brought in in Christ. But "since the law and the prophets were until John" who pointed out Christ, therefore I think it is said that vision and prophet are sealed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For since there are by no means visions among the prophets after John, therefore vision and prophet have been sealed. And vision and prophet being sealed, the only-begotten holy of holies Christ was anointed. Which Christ the anointed one the prophets and Daniel came to know, and understood in some manner "from the going forth of the word", when "by the word of the Lord the heavens were established".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And "from the going forth of the word to answer" in the saints who were from the beginning and the prophets of the Lord, but also "to build Jerusalem unto Christ the leader" there passed "sixty-two weeks": that is, first indeed four hundred and ninety years, which are made by the decades of the seven weeks reckoned, but after this four thousand three hundred and forty years, which are likewise made by the decades of the sixty-two weeks reckoned. After which Christ returned, and built the street in which wisdom "acts with confidence", and the wall on whose summit "he is proclaimed". But the times of the people were emptied out, on account of which, upon the sixty-two weeks added to the seven weeks, the chrism which was in the temple was taken away from the people, so that there might now no longer be judgment among them. But both the city and the sanctuary were corrupted with the leader coming afterward upon that people, whether Herod or Agrippa (for the history of the Jews says it is this man).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But see that you do not suppose that what he says, that it is corrupted "with the leader who comes", is referred to Christ; for where he wished him to be understood as Christ, Daniel used both names, saying "unto Christ the leader", but when he keeps silent the name of Christ, he brings in a leader who is to corrupt, since the leader failed after Christ, and "the leader from his thighs", for he came "for whom the things were laid up". After whom the people was cut off "in a flood" "unto the end of the war" cut short upon them. But these things happening to them, God confirmed "the covenant to many" in one week: in the middle of which week he caused the incense and the sacrifices and the temple to cease (which I think he named from the pinnacle) that was to perish "unto the consummation" in haste, when also their house was forsaken to them who sinned.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the things which follow in the text of Daniel we have expounded as best we could. And all these things it has seemed good to us to set forth from Daniel alongside the interpretation of the Gospel text, so that we may make plain the saying which he speaks: when you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place, let him who reads it understand.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Whence I think that by the abomination of desolation, He means the army by which the city of the holy Jerusalem was desolated.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (Verse 16 onwards) Then those who are in Judea, let them flee to the mountains; and those who are on the roof, let them not come down to take anything from their house; and those who are in the field, let them not turn back to take their cloak.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: The abomination of desolation can be understood, and every perverse teaching; when we see it standing in the holy place, that is, in the Church, and proclaiming itself as God, we must flee from Judea to the mountains, that is, leaving behind the letter of the law and Jewish corruption, and approach the eternal mountains, from which God wonderfully enlightens (Psalms 75); and be on the roof and in the inner room, where the fiery darts of the devil cannot reach: neither coming down and taking anything from the former way of life: nor turning back are they to seek; but rather to sow in the field of spiritual Scriptures, so that we may bear fruit from it. Neither to take off the other tunic, which the apostles are forbidden to have. On this subject, that is, on the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by the prophet Daniel, Porphyry blasphemed against us in the thirteenth volume of his work, while standing in a holy place.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: To him, Eusebius of Caesarea, the bishop, responded in three volumes: the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth. Apollinaris ((also known as Apollinarius)) also wrote extensively, and attempted to discuss in one chapter what has been disputed in so many thousands of verses.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Having spoken of the ills that were to overtake the city, and of the trials of the apostles, and that they should remain unsubdued, and should overrun the whole world, He mentions again the Jews' calamities, showing that when the one should be glorious, having taught the whole world, the others should be in calamity.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 76

paragraphs.text: And see how He relates the war, by the things that seem to be small setting forth how intolerable it was to be. For, "Then," saith He, "let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains." Then, When? When these things should be, "when the abomination of desolation should stand in the holy place."
